item.title: In 1956, Tressa Prisbrey turned discarded bottles into a 15-building folk-art village in California
item.description: Tressa Prisbrey, at age 60, began building Bottle Village using glass bottles from a local landfill. Over 25 years, she constructed 15 unique structures dedicated to her lost children and their memories. The site eventually became a cultural landmark and received various recognitions for its artistic significance. Visitors paid small admission fees to see her creative work and hear her story. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: Alice Waters’ school garden project grew into a global network of 5,800 programmes across 75 countries
item.description: Launched back in 1995 in California, the Edible Schoolyard Project has blossomed into a global initiative founded by chef Alice Waters. The project imparts essential lessons on gardening and environmental stewardship, seamlessly integrating with subjects like science and math. With a mission to foster healthy eating habits, it has inspired educational platforms across more than 75 countries, aiming to weave food education into everyday school curricula for enhanced student wellbeing. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: Modeling study shows early tetrapods had surprisingly little ability to move their necks
item.description: A new model using sturgeon as a material analog has made it possible to estimate how the backbones of some of the first animals on land could and could not move. These results disprove a long-standing hypothesis that changes in early tetrapod anatomy as they moved onto land gave them improved neck mobility. The study, led by a researcher at Uppsala University, formerly of Carleton University in Canada, has been published in the journal Nature. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New Yorker’s $3 yard sale bowl sells for $2.2 million
item.description: A remarkable discovery unfolded in 2007 when a New Yorker purchased a small white bowl for merely three dollars during a yard sale. For years, this bowl was displayed proudly in their home until appraisers revealed its true worth: a rare 'Ding' ware from the Northern Song dynasty valued between $200,000 to $300,000.
